paper_title: Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) can succeed with surprisingly few training questions, motivating a view of questions as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer. How can we assess whether a newly generated question is valuable for distillation, and learn to generate better questions---without access to its correct answer? We introduce Ask-to-Distill (\method), a framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors and optimizes the teacher supervision they expose along student-generated trajectories. A student-initialized synthesizer is optimized using a distributional surrogate for question value, computed from a frozen student--teacher pair without reference answers, correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates. The reward combines teacher--student disagreement with teacher probability mass on the student's candidate support, together with length and diversity controls. The generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into a prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, our method improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision and more total signal from shorter student responses, supporting elicited distributional supervision as an objective for synthetic distillation data. Our code, data and models are publicly available at https://github.com/GasolSun36/Ask_to_Distill.

Introduction On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers the behavior of strong teacher to student on trajectories sampled by the student itself (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). By supervising the states the student actually visits, OPD mitigates the distribution mismatch associated with learning only from fixed teacher demonstrations and provides dense token-level guidance without requiring task-specific corAsk to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation rectness verifier. Although the teacher supplies this supervision, the training questions determine which trajectories the student generates and where teacher feedback becomes available. Constructing effective distillation data therefore requires understanding not only what question asks, but also what supervision it elicits from particular student teacher pair. Recent studies suggest that OPD can be highly promptefficient: small subsets can approach full-data performance, and even single question can recover much of the gain obtained from large question bank (Fu et al., 2026; Hou et al., 2026). Moreover, self-generated questions can support effective OPD without external seed examples (Li et al., 2026a). These findings motivate different perspective on OPD training data, centered on the supervision that questions elicit. In supervised fine-tuning, synthetic examples provide target responses for imitation (Wang et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024); in self-play reinforcement learning, generated tasks provide opportunities to learn from answer-quality or task-success feedback (Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025). OPD instead obtains supervision from the teachers token distributions on student-generated prefixes. question therefore serves as distribution elicitor: it guides the student into states where teacherstudent differences become available for learning. From this perspective, training questions act as carriers of distributional knowledge transfer, rather than directly supplying the target knowledge through reference answers. Their distillation value depends on the usable teacher supervision exposed along the induced trajectories for particular studentteacher pair, consistent with findings that prompt utility is pair-dependent (Wang et al., 2026a). Although OPD supplies teacher supervision without reference answers, optimizing question synthesizer requires an additional signal: feedback on which questions are worth generating. This raises central question: without access to the correct answer to newly generated question, how can we assess its value for target studentteacher pair and use that assessment to learn to generate better questions? We address this question by scoring the distributional supervision exposed along student-generated trajectories, using frozen studentteacher pair without performing student update for each candidate. Turning elicited supervision into an optimization objective requires distinguishing disagreement from useful correction. Token-selection and reweighting methods already exploit the unequal value of supervision across response positions (Xu et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026b). In particular, support-aware analyses of token teachability show that large divergence can reflect either corrective teacher preferences within the students candidate support or mismatch concentrated outside that support (Wang et al., 2026b). Building on this characterization, we combine teacherstudent discrepancy with teacher probability mass on the students candidate tokens as surrogate for local learning value. We adapt this token-level principle to question generation by aggregating the signal along student trajectories. This introduces additional challenges: synthesizer may increase its reward through longer responses or repeatedly produce narrow family of questions. The question-level objective must therefore balance elicited signal with trajectory length and question diversity. We introduce Ask-to-Distill (A2D), self-contained framework that optimizes synthetic questions for target student teacher pair before performing OPD. We initialize the question-generation policy from the student and train it with reinforcement learning, while keeping the scoring student and teacher frozen. Its reward aggregates support-aware token signals using sublinear length normalization, soft response-budget penalty, and batch-diversity term. We then curate the generated questions through format filtering and lexical and semantic deduplication, and perform standard OPD on the resulting prompt-only dataset. Synthesizer training reuses the target studentteacher pair and requires neither external training questions nor auxiliary models. After training, frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B model is used only for semantic deduplication of the generated question bank; it does not participate in synthesizer optimization. Our method operates on the prompt-construction axis, which is complementary to approaches that select supervision positions, reweight trajectories, or modify the downstream distillation procedure. Our contributions are threefold: (i) we formulate synthetic prompt construction as optimizing the distributional supervision elicited from target studentteacher pair; (ii) we develop question-level reward that turns support-aware teacherstudent signals into feedback for synthesizer optimization, without reference answers, task-specific correctness rewards, or per-candidate student updates, while controlling response length and question diversity; and (iii) we validate the framework across multiple model scales and mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks through downstream comparisons, reward-component ablations, and learning-signal analyses. A2D exceeds real-bank OPD on the average scores of the evaluated studentteacher pairs. Our analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser distributional signals from shorter student responses, supporting the value of optimizing elicited supervision beyond simply increasing rollout length. 2. Main Results We evaluate A2D across six mathematical reasoning and six code-generation benchmarks, with three studentteacher pairs in each domain. Tables 1 and 2 report the main results. Across all six settings, A2D achieves the highest average performance among the compared distillation methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of optimizing synthetic questions for the target studentteacher pair. Mathematical reasoning. As shown in Table 1, A2D achieves average scores of 46.2, 51.6, and 64.5 for Qwen31.7B, R1-Distill-1.5B, and R1-Distill-7B, respectively, compared with 43.0, 50.5, and 62.9 for Vanilla OPD. These results show that optimized synthetic questions can outperform the original real question bank across both nonthinking and reasoning students. The corresponding teachergap recovery rates reach 90.2%, 99.9%, and 81.3%; notably, R1-Distill-1.5B nearly matches its teachers average performance. Relative to Student-Generated OPD, our method improves the reported average scores by 5.1, 3.4, and 3.7 percentage points, indicating that optimizing the synthesizer provides additional value beyond sampling questions directly from the student. 10 Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation age performance, and achieves the best or tied-best score among the compared distillation methods in 16 of the 18 benchmarkpair combinations. The gains extend across multiple coding benchmarks. For example, with Qwen330B-A3B as the teacher, APPS-Interview improves from 21.3 to 31.6 and CodeContests from 4.8 to 13.9 relative to Vanilla OPD. These results extend the benefits of optimizing elicited supervision beyond mathematical reasoning to code generation. The magnitude of improvement nevertheless varies substantially across studentteacher pairs. Teacher-gap recovery reaches 82.9% for Qwen3-4B distilled from the 4B teacher, but remains at 32.8% with the stronger 30B-A3B teacher and 12.3% for the Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/32B pair. Moreover, for the same Qwen3-4B student, the stronger teacher yields lower distilled average score than the 4B teacher under our setup. This comparison indicates that teacher benchmark performance alone does not determine downstream distillation effectiveness. Optimizing the question distribution consistently improves the evaluated outcomes, while substantial headroom remains in some studentteacher settings. 3.5. Ablation: Can stronger model replace synthetic data optimization? natural alternative to training synthesizer for each studentteacher pair is to ask stronger off-the-shelf model in our setting, the teacher itselfto generate the questions. To separate the effect of synthesizer initialization from that of pair-specific optimization, we compare studentand teacher-initialized synthesizers, each with and without RL, while holding the downstream distillation setup fixed. Figure 3 reports performance over training for representative code studentteacher pair; the dashed lines mark the student and teacher reference scores. Without RL, teacher initialization improves over student initialization on the two APPS subsets, but not on LCB, and neither unoptimized synthesizer matches the student-initialized RL variant across the three benchmarks. Applying RL improves the trajectories for both initializations, indicating that the benefit is not explained by simply prompting stronger model to write questions. The student-initialized RL variant reaches roughly 35% on LCB, above the teacher reference of 33.7%, and about 62% on APPS-Intro. On APPS-Interview it reaches about 36%; both APPS scores remain below their teacher references (65.6% and 41.0%, respectively). The teacher-initialized RL variant is competitiveand slightly higher at some APPS-Intro checkpointsbut does not consistently dominate the student-initialized variant. Thus, synthesizer strength alone is not substitute for optimizing questions against the target pair, while the choice of initialization can still affect performance by benchmark. Ablation: which reward components matter? We ablate compatibility, the training-time diversity term, and the explicit length penalty, and evaluate the resulting question banks by downstream best accuracy on AIME24, AIME25, and AIME26 (Figure 4). The full reward performs best on all three benchmarks, reaching 45.0%, 35.8%, and 29.2%, respectively. On AIME25, removing compatibility, diversity, or the length penalty reduces accuracy by 6.2, 6.0, and 6.6 points, respectively. On AIME24, the largest reduction is 4.2 points without diversity; on AIME26, it is 3.4 points without the length penalty. These results suggest that all three components contribute to the performance of the complete reward, while their relative importance varies across benchmarks. Table 3 reports results for Qwen3-4B (non-thinking). Our method reaches 46.3%, 49.4%, and 30.0% in the three domains, respectively, for an average of 41.9%. This exceeds Student-Generated OPD by 3.8, 6.9, and 3.1 percentage points, respectively (4.6 points on average), and raises teacher-gap recovery from 79.2% to 95.2%. It also outperforms Vanilla OPD (40.4% average) and KL-Filtered OPD (40.9%) on the average score. For this studentteacher pair, these results support the applicability of pair-specific 12 Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation question optimization to agentic task domains as well as to reasoning and code generation. Cross-Domain Transfer between Math and Code Our distribution-elicitation perspective suggests that the benefits of OPD need not be confined to the domain of its training questions. We examine this hypothesis in two directions: code-to-math transfer with Qwen3-4B (non-thinking) distilled from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, and math-to-code transfer with R1-Distill-7B distilled from Skywork-OR1Math-7B. In each setting, we directly evaluate the student after source-domain OPD, without additional target-domain training, comparing our optimized synthetic questions with the real source-domain questions used by Vanilla OPD. We report gains over the initial student and compute an unweighted average across the target benchmarks. Code-to-math transfer. We evaluate code-trained students on AIME24, AIME26, AMC23, and BRUMO25. As shown in Figure 7(a), both methods improve performance on all four mathematics benchmarks. A2D raises average accuracy from 31.38% to 38.60%, gain of 7.23 percentage points, compared with 5.33 points for Vanilla OPD. Our method consistently yields larger improvements across the four benchmarks, with gains of 11.0, 5.2, 8.5, and 4.2 points, respectively. These results show that supervision elicited by code questions can also benefit mathematical reasoning. Math-to-code transfer. We evaluate mathematics-trained students on LiveCodeBench, APPS-Intro, and APPSInterview. Figure 7(b) shows that A2D improves performance by 2.7, 4.8, and 8.7 percentage points, respectively, compared with 1.9, 3.8, and 6.7 points for Vanilla OPD. Average accuracy increases from 47.00% to 52.40% with our method, exceeding Vanilla OPDs 51.13% and approaching the teachers 52.70%. The student also surpasses the teacher on APPS-Intro (70.1% versus 68.7%), while remaining below it on the other two benchmarks. Together, these results demonstrate cross-domain gains in both evaluated directions, with our optimized synthetic questions outperforming real source-domain questions on every reported target benchmark. This finding is consistent with questions serving as carriers of distributional supervision whose benefits extend beyond the training domain. Although these experiments do not isolate the mechanism underlying transfer, they show that optimizing the supervision elicited from particular studentteacher pair can improve performance beyond source-domain tasks. 13 3.9. Iterative Training Our main framework optimizes synthetic questions for fixed studentteacher pair before performing OPD. We further examine whether repeating this process as the student improves yields additional benefits. We conduct three rounds on the code-generation pair consisting of Qwen34B student and Qwen3-30B-A3B teacher. After each round, we update the student used for question optimization, construct new synthetic question bank, and continue OPD while keeping the teacher fixed. We evaluate on LiveCodeBench, APPS-Intro, and APPS-Interview and report the highest observed average accuracy across the evaluated checkpoints within each round. This comparison provides an optimistic assessment of the benefits of additional rounds, rather than validation-selected final result. The first round raises average accuracy from 29.03% to 40.53%, an improvement of 11.50 percentage points. Best-of-N Teacher Rollout Selection augments student-context supervision with an auxiliary teacher trajectory selected according to correctness and student alignment (Zhang et al., 2026). PromptKD instead tunes teacherside prompts to produce student-friendly supervision (Kim et al., 2024). These approaches modify how supervision is produced or delivered, whereas our method learns the questions that elicit it. Selective OPD further recognizes that response positions provide unequal learning value. TIP characterizes token importance through student entropy and teacherstudent divergence (Xu et al., 2026). Entropy-Aware OPD augments reverse KL with forward KL at high-teacher-entropy positions (Jin et al., 2026), and FiRe-OPD combines trajectory filtering with soft token reweighting (Li et al., 2026b). Token Teachability distinguishes locally learnable disagreement from mismatch outside the students candidate support, using teacherstudent discrepancy and teacher probability mass on the students top-K candidates (Wang et al., 2026b). In the related setting of on-policy self-distillation, matching supervision to student capacity has also been studied through joint token weighting and privileged-information adjustment (Yang et al., 2026b). We build on the supportaware characterization of teachability, adapting it into question-level reward with trajectory aggregation, length control, and batch-diversity control. Our optimization changes the synthetic prompt distribution while holding the downstream OPD procedure fixed. 4.2. Synthetic Data Generation and Selection for Distillation Synthetic-data methods differ in the feedback used to construct training examples. Self-Instruct generates instruction response pairs for supervised finetuning (Wang et al., 2023), and WizardLM evolves instructions toward greater complexity (Xu et al., 2024). R-Zero and Self-Questioning Language Models train task proposers through solver feedback to support self-improving reasoning (Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2025). Self-Adapting Language Models learns to generate finetuning data and update directives using the adapted models downstream performance (Zweiger et al., 2025). Particularly relevant to our setting, Prompting to Distill uses reinforced prompts and teacherstudent discrepancy to synthesize data for text-classification distillation (Ma et al., 2022). Our work extends the broader idea of feedback-guided synthesis to prompt-only OPD data, where value is assessed through teacher distributions along student-generated reasoning trajectories. Recent studies directly examine the role of training questions in OPD. Rethinking OPD identifies teacherstudent compatibility as an important factor and proposes teacheraligned prompt selection (Li et al., 2026c). Its follow-up shows that single query can expose broad state coverage and recover much of the gain from full-data training (Fu et al., 2026). What Matters in OPD studies difficulty-based selection, finding that small set of hard questions can match much larger dataset in its evaluated settings and relating their utility to longer reasoning trajectories (Hou et al., 2026). Beyond Prompt Count shows that prompt usefulness depends on the studentteacher pair and target capability, with targeted selection not consistently outperforming random sampling (Wang et al., 2026a). Data-Free OPD further demonstrates effective distillation using self-generated questions without external seed examples (Li et al., 2026a). A2D learns synthesizer to actively shape the question distribution for target studentteacher pair. Its objective evaluates the support-aware supervision elicited by each question, rather than using surface complexity, answer correctness, or raw disagreement alone as the generation criterion. Unlike selection from an existing question bank or direct sampling from an unoptimized model, our pipeline trains the synthesizer using frozen scoring pair and then constructs 16 Ask to Distill: Learning to Synthesize Data for On-Policy Distillation curated prompt-only bank for OPD. Question generation and synthesizer training reuse the target student and teacher without external training questions or auxiliary models. frozen embedding model is used only to remove semantically redundant questions during post-generation curation. 5. Conclusion We introduced A2D, framework that treats synthetic questions as distribution elicitors for on-policy distillation. Rather than judging question by its surface form, A2D trains student-initialized synthesizer against frozen studentteacher pair to expose useful teacher supervision along student-generated trajectories. Its learning-value reward combines teacherstudent disagreement with teacher probability mass on the students candidate support, together with length and diversity controls, and the generated questions are filtered and deduplicated into prompt-only bank for standard OPD. Synthesizer training reuses the target student and teacher without external training questions or auxiliary models; frozen embedding model is used only for post-generation semantic deduplication. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and agentic tasks, A2D improves average performance and teacher-gap recovery over unoptimized student-generated prompts and KL-filtered real questions, while matching or exceeding real-bank OPD in the evaluated settings. Signal analyses further show that optimized questions can elicit denser supervision from shorter student responses. These results support elicited distributional supervision as an objective for constructing synthetic distillation data. Our learning-value reward is surrogate estimated from single student response per question, and the synthesizer is optimized once for fixed studentteacher pair. Developing more effective adaptive question-generation strategies as the student improves, and combining learned question generation with token-level selection methods for OPD, are natural directions for future work.

For reward computation, we use = 16 candidate tokens, question-generation budget of Lq = 4096 tokens, and student-response budget of Lmax = 7168 tokens, with the latter matched to the downstream OPD response budget by construction (2.6). For each studentteacher pair, the discrepancy scale δref is set to the κ = 95th percentile of δt estimated from Ncal = 200 questions, and we use ϵ = 108 in Eq. (6). For reward shaping, we set the aggregation exponent α = 0.5, the length-penalty coefficient λlen = 0.3, the diversity-penalty coefficient λdiv = 1.0, and the clustering threshold τ = 0.1. The synthetic-data synthesizer is optimized with GRPO using 8 prompts and group size of = 8, yielding 64 candidate questions per step. We use learning rate of 1 106, entropy and KL coefficients of 0.01 and 0.005, respectively, and rollout temperature of 1.0, training for 60 steps and saving checkpoints every 5 steps. We generate = 20,000 raw questions in 10 shards of 2000 samples each and apply Jaccard and cosine deduplication thresholds of τlex = 0.7 and τsem = 0.95, respectively. Downstream OPD uses token-level rewards directly as advantages, with the students top-K candidates (K = 16) weighted by pS. We sample nroll = 4 responses per prompt at temperature 1.0 and train with batch size of 64, learning rate of 1 106, and fp32 parameters for 2 epochs, saving checkpoints every 5 steps. For each studentteacher pair and each OPD method, we select single downstream student checkpoint based on AMC23 performance for mathematical reasoning and LiveCodeBench performance for code generation. All benchmark scores reported for that method are evaluated at this same checkpoint, rather than selected independently for each benchmark. AMC23 and LiveCodeBench therefore serve as checkpoint-selection benchmarks; their reported scores are not held-out estimates. A.3. Evaluation Details Metric. For each benchmark, we sample responses per problem and report avg@k: the fraction of correct responses for each problem, averaged over problems and scaled to [0, 100]. With = 1, this reduces to single-sample accuracy. All reported results are means over three independent runs with different random seeds. The reported averages weight each benchmark equally, regardless of its number of problems. Table 5 lists the per-benchmark settings. All evaluations use vLLM (v0.11.0) (Kwon et al., 2023) with bf16 inference on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. Mathematical reasoning. We use the DAPO prompt format, which asks the model to reason step by step and to give its final answer within boxed{}. Qwen3 students and teachers are evaluated in non-thinking mode, whereas DeepSeekR1-Distill students and their teachers (JustRL and Skywork-OR1) use their default thinking templates. We extract the last boxed{} expression, falling back to the last Answer: line, and verify it against the reference answer by rule-based string normalization and symbolic equivalence checking with SymPy (Meurer et al., 2017); no model-based judge is used. Code generation. For LiveCodeBench, we use the v5v6 release subset of 342 problems published between September 2024 and April 2025, with the original LiveCodeBench prompt. For APPS, we use the full introductory and competition test splits (1,000 problems each) and 1,000 interview problems drawn from the test split with fixed random seed, keeping at most 50 test cases per problem; prompts follow the LiveCodeBench standard-input template. MBPP+ uses EvalPlus v0.2.0 (378 problems) with its standard prompt template and greedy decoding. Qwen3 models are evaluated in non-thinking mode. We extract the last fenced code block from each response and execute it against all test cases; response is counted as correct only if it passes every test within the time limit. In the math-to-code transfer experiment (Figure 7), the Qwen3 models use the non-thinking settings in Table 5, whereas DeepSeek-R1-Distill students and their mathematics teachers are evaluated in thinking mode with their default chat templates, using temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, and maximum generation length of 32,768 tokens on all three benchmarks.
